speechtext: Mr. Speaker, today, according to reports in the media, a committee of the House wants the Government to impose a tax on food. Mr. Speaker, I would like to make it clear that as far as the Liberal Party is concerned, there is not going to be a tax on bread and butter. That is our position. At the request of my Leader (Mr. Turner), my colleague from Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) and I circulated petitions across Canada, and Canadians are entirely against the introduction of this new tax. However, I warn the Canadians who are listening that I would not be surprised if the Government, considering the way it and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) deceived senior citizens in the matter of deindexing old age security pensions, I would not be surprised that if this Government is ever re-elected, the first thing it would do would be to put a tax on bread and butter. Don't trust them!

Mr. Speaker, the United Kingdom Government of Margaret Thatcher must be congratulated for reporting a budgetary surplus yesterday of some three billion pounds. This compares to Canada's $29-billion deficit. The burning question is why Canada spends so much more than it raises.
Not one day passes but we parliamentarians are lobbied to spend more, be it by industry, by commerce, or by special interest groups. Not surprisingly, no one lobbies us for higher taxes.
This credit card mentality must change. We as a society cannot afford to spend money we do not have. A continuation of our current policy can only lead to higher interest rates, a declining dollar, and monetary chaos. The choice is simple, prudence now or chaos later.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS BRITISH COLUMBIA THRONE SPEECH-AWARDING OF FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS BRITISH COLUMBIA THRONE SPEECH-AWARDING OF FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday's British Columbia Throne Speech shows that Premier Bill Vander Zalm has changed his buddy-buddy relationship with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and is now trying to talk tough in order to get fair shares for British Columbia. It is true that British Columbia has not received its fair share of federal contracts.
Of the 30 largest contractors ranked in terms of the dollar value of contracts received, only one was a British Columbia firm. British Columbia has 11.4 per cent of the population but in 1986-87 B.C. suppliers got only 9.1 per cent of federal government contracts, down from 10.2 per cent in 1985-86. These were relatively small purchases amounting to only 4.1 per cent of total federal purchasing outlays, down from 5.3 per cent in 1985-86.
British Columbians do not want a Premier who is a sycophant, they do not want a Premier who attempts to be a bully, they do not want a Premier who is the cry-baby of Confederation. They want someone who will stand up, speak reasonably, and get a fair deal for British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, human life in whatever form is sacred. It is precious and must be protected by the full force and effect of the law from the very moment of conception to natural death. Just as it is wrong for the state to allow the taking of a life through capital punishment, it is equally wrong to take a life before birth.

March 16, 1988
Parliament, each and every one of us, will soon have to decide when life begins. There is only one logical and just answer. Life begins at conception. To conclude that life begins at any other stage is to demean the very essence of life.
The Charter of Rights and Freedoms does not discriminate between human beings. Regardless of how tragic or miserable or physically or mentally impaired a life is, that life is protected by law. We all have the right to life. Why, then, should we discriminate prior to birth? It is morally wrong to do so.
To quote an individual who wrote to all of us: "Just as one cannot be a little bit pregnant or a little bit honourable or a little bit honest or a little bit faithful, a country cannot have a Constitution that holds that life is a little bit sacred. It is either protected or it is not protected."
The most important human right, the only absolute human right, is the right to life. I hope Parliament endorses this principle during the abortion debate.

subsubtopic: SAVINGS ACHIEVED THROUGH GOVERNMENT'S CASH MANAGEMENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was recently announced that, due to the Government's improvement in cash management practices, over $539 million has been saved since 1985. These savings are projected to reach $1.2 billion by 1991, illuminating the positive impact that modern business-like practices can have on government. It is interesting to note that this story made page 13 in The Ottawa Citizen last week.
The savings in taxpayers' dollars do not become apparent overnight. It took time for management to assess the situation and introduce new practices. Now the benefits of an increasingly efficient federal Government are starting to yield real savings. These savings represent the fact that Government does not have to continue down the path of increasing growth and waste.
The introduction of practices like prompt bank deposits and paying suppliers on time was the kind of common sense needed in the financial management of the country. I have worked for sound financial management in government on the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, and I know the Government will continue to do more to ensure better use of taxpayers' dollars.

East): Mr. Speaker, I was the Solicitor General in 1974 when the decision was made to admit women to the RCMP and, as a result, I was extremely disappointed today to read that their status in the force is not improving but worsening. At present there are 852 female constables in the RCMP constituting 6.5 per cent of all constables. When women were admitted to this male stronghold in 1974 it was recognized that special steps would have to be taken to facilitate their participation, as was done by many police forces in North America and Europe. subsubtopic: LOSS OF NOVA SCOTIA FISHERMEN'S LIVES-DUTY TO ASSIST FAMILIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for generations the villagers of Sambro have sailed from their safe harbour to fish on the treacherous waters of the North Atlantic. The risks are immense and ever present, but fishing is not merely a vocation but a way of life for many Maritimers.
On March 8, 1988, the dangers of ocean fishing struck the crew of the Bonnie Lou II. A late winter storm attacked this small vessel causing damage that led to its destruction. The sea search that followed failed to find any trace of the five young crewmen. Skipper Lome Gray, brothers Jimmie and Brian Gray, Denny Gilkie and Blair Gray were lost on the North Atlantic. Family and friends were forced to conclude that these brave young fishermen were victims of the raging ocean.
The fishermen of Sambro will continue to challenge the Atlantic Ocean despite the risks because fishing is their way of life. Parliamentarians and all Canadians moved by this tragedy will recognize a duty to ensure their families and children are helped and protected.

subtopic: S'. O. 21 APARTHEID SOUTH AFRICA-DENUNCIATION OF DECISION TO EXECUTE "THE SHARPEVILLE SIX"
S'. O. 21 APARTHEID SOUTH AFRICA-DENUNCIATION OF DECISION TO EXECUTE "THE SHARPEVILLE SIX"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is one of those days when I regret the passing of the old Standing Order 43, because today is the kind of day on which all Members of this House might have been able to join, through that procedure, in unanimously urging the Government of South Africa to commute the hanging sentences of "the Sharpeville Six".
However, we do not have that procedure available to us so we must get up, time and again-the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), and every one of us-to make it absolutely clear that we regard as abominable the decision of the South African Government to hang these six individuals, which decision contravenes every principle of liberal and democratic jurisprudence which we could imagine.
It sets a bad precedent that blacks in South Africa in particular can be sentenced to be hanged on the basis of their participation in a crowd rather than on the basis of that for which they can individually be held responsible. It certainly shows once again that the Government of South Africa intends to use every device at its disposal to combat anti-apartheid activity. That is something which all Canadians reject.

Mr. Speaker, on February 10, Brian Grant, an employee with Revenue Canada, was suspended for passing information to two government agencies. The information led Immigration Canada to apprehend 24 illegal aliens as well as providing the police with a vital piece of evidence which led to solving a murder.
Because of these acts Mr. Grant is now subject to an investigation for breach of confidentiality. This is a serious matter and one which must be addressed. A policy must be implemented whereby individuals in Departments can communicate information to their superiors which is detrimental to Canadians. In addition, a clear policy of inter-agency communications must be implemented. All government Departments and agencies must have one goal of ensuring that the safety and well-being of Canadians come first.



March 16, 1988
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the Ontario Environment Minister, Mr. Jim Bradley, told the King of Sweden: "The polluters in the United States and the United Kingdom are waging environmental war on our countries", because Ontario and Sweden are both threatened by acid rain coming from neighbours upwind who refuse to cut pollution. Mr. Bradley pointed out: "This situation will continue and worsen unless we find the means to make a great change in the actions of our neighbours".
Mr. Bradley called upon the United States and Britain to join Canada and Sweden in the 30 Per Cent Club, a group of over 20 nations which have vowed to cut S02 emissions by at least 30 per cent by 1994. It is refreshing to hear a Canadian speaking up on the international acid rain perspective. Unfortunately, it is a provincial environment Minister alone who has the vision to speak up.
The federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is silent on the international acid rain stage. Perhaps Mr. Bradley's remarks will give the federal Minister the courage to speak up now.

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party and Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) is taking a negative approach to free trade, although he is fully aware of the fact that the agreement will boost the Canadian economy and create jobs.
For 25 years now his riding has benefitted from the automotive agreement under which Ontario has recorded Canada's lowest unemployment rate-5.8 per cent-and created the highest number of jobs, while central Quebec had to cope with an unemployment level in excess of 10 per cent.

subsubtopic: SERVICE FEES CHARGED BY BANKS AND TRUST COMPANIES
speechtext:

Would the Minister explain to Canadians the fairness and appropriateness of the Royal Trust charging consumers a fee if their balance is too low? Would he explain why the Bank of Montreal charges a fee if one wants information on one's own account? And would he explain why the Bank of Nova Scotia and the Toronto Dominion Bank have retroactive service charge fees? In other words, one is informed in July of a service charge that took place in June.
Would the Minister explain to Canadians the fairness of these measures and why he continues to allow them to exist? Why does he do that?

speechtext: I want to advise Hon. Members that we have a question of privilege to deal with. I call first on the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I raised a question of privilege in connection with reports which were under consideration by the Finance Committee which had, unfortunately, been allowed to get into the public hand improperly and without the permission of the committee. They were released in such a fashion as to cause some concern to the public.
As a result of a young man coming forward, that issue has now, I think, been resolved. We have received advice from the young man, who was an employee of a Member. I know the young man and I think he has learned his lesson. I think, Sir, that if you would outline as far as possible the views of the Chair on this matter, we would probably best handle it in that fashion and not proceed further by referring this specific matter to the Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure, although it is clearly a matter of privilege because of the damage that the release of confidential material can cause, not only to the committee but to the House itself and to the integrity of Members.
Privilege-Mr. Blenkarn
I think this particular matter has been attended to and dealt with effectively, but if you could make a ruling on the issue, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be appreciated by all Members of the House.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED LEAK OF CONFIDENTIAL RESEARCH MATERIAL OF STANDING COMMITTEE-RULING OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to express, in the strongest possible terms, my disapproval of what has happened. When a preliminary draft prepared by a staff person is misrepresented as a report by Members of Parliament, it is not only mischievous but a serious obstruction to the continuing work of the committee. The real report will not get the same media attention as the leaked draft and some Canadians will remain misinformed. This is particularly irresponsible, even cruel, in the matter of the sales tax on food.
All three Parties in this House have taken a position against imposing a sales tax on food. Yet, this morning's headlines screamed something different. My colleagues from Newfoundland tell me that there were radio shows in their areas beamed into very poor areas telling people that their food bills were about to go up by 10 per cent.
I can hardly find words to express my disapproval of the irresponsibility which would impose that kind of pain and distress on poor people who are finding it hard enough to live.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED LEAK OF CONFIDENTIAL RESEARCH MATERIAL OF STANDING COMMITTEE-RULING OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

A less important matter, although I still mention it, is that the same staff person who released this draft report on the committee's examination of the sales tax in New Zealand before the committee had expressed opinion on it, also released to the press a draft report on banking charges, again to which the committee had not yet bent its mind.

There is nothing wrong with a preliminary draft being less than accurate because obviously the staff keeps reviewing and checking for accuracy, with or without the input of members of the committee. Although I would not be quite as kind as the Chairman about the young staff person involved, and I agree he is young and young people are entitled to make mistakes once-let us hope he has learned from it-I agree he should not be named

or pilloried. However,he is not only an individual working for a Member of Parliament, he has also worked for our committee for six months. He is in a position to know very well the difference between a preliminary draft prepared by staff at which Members have not looked and a report that Members are in the process of adopting. For someone with that kind of inside information to hand out a draft to the media as a final draft is triply irresponsible and deserving of condemnation.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED LEAK OF CONFIDENTIAL RESEARCH MATERIAL OF STANDING COMMITTEE-RULING OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our Party, I also want to express disapproval over what has happened. What has happened is wrong. It is wrong for someone, be it a Member of Parliament or a staff member from an office of a Member of Parliament, to leak confidential information to the press. I think this is the time we should remind ourselves that this place runs because of trust. Yes, we have partisan politics and we differ on issues, but Parliament only runs because there is a certain amount of trust between the members of all political Parties.
I want to compliment the generous comments of the Chairman of the finance committee, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). He says he knows the person in question and he thinks that person has learned his lesson. I too know the person in question and I do think this person has learned his lesson. However, that aside, I think this is a very important opportunity to remind all Members of Parliament and to remind the staff of Members of Parliament that when we are dealing with confidential work in the House of Commons, or in the committees of the House of Commons, that work should remain confidential. If it does not, it undermines the trust of this place and the integrity of all Members of Parliament.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLEGED LEAK OF CONFIDENTIAL RESEARCH MATERIAL OF STANDING COMMITTEE-RULING OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Hon. Members have just heard the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and others. The effect of their interventions has been to inform this House that a member of the staff of a Member of Parliament has admitted leaking confidential and private research material from the finance committee to the print media.
As your Speaker, it is my humble opinion that it is in the best interests of the House that this matter now be set aside, given the fact that Members of Parliament from all three Parties who sit on the committee have made the remarks they have in this place.
However, this issue does warrant some comment from the Chair, and it is with caution that any presiding officer comments on such matters. First, let me express my personal gratitude to Members for the manner in which this was handled. Honour and trust, even in as difficult and sometimes as partisan an arena as this, is the foundation of our democratic system of government. The House of Commons can only be effective when the basic principles of honesty and trust guide its often heated debates.
I wish to remind those who work for Members that while they enjoy some of the privileges of the House, they also bear,
in our more modern parliamentary system, the very heavy responsibilities of trust, honour and confidentiality. It is rare indeed that such matters have occupied the time of this House and, given all that goes on on Parliament Hill, it is a credit to all those people who serve us so well that such incidents are the extreme exception.
I must say to all Hon. Members, and to everyone who works in this place for Hon. Members, that if it had not been for the frank explanation and the way in which all three Members on this committee, representing all three Parties, have intervened, this breach of privilege could easily have been referred to the appropriate committee with all the consequences that would ensue.
However, there was another participant in this incident. The confidential report of the finance committee may well have been released without proper authorization as, in fact, of course, it was, but someone else also decided to print or report parts thereof. The new, reformed committees of the House have greater powers than ever before. They are now inquiring more often into areas of vital public interest. The Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), in what, I think, was an extremely lucid intervention, has pointed out exactly the harm to the public interest that flows from either the irresponsible leaking of material or the injudicious use of it once it is leaked.
To ensure that these committees are able to function in a climate of trust, Members are agreed that their work should not be impeded, delayed or obstructed or brought under undue suspicion by any premature publication of their in camera proceedings or draft reports. The good relations between the House and the media are also founded on principles of trust and honour. Those of us who have spent time in this place know that it is impossible to have a democratic community unless there is that relationship between those who are elected and those who report on us.
I can only hope that in the future, the media might reflect on the conventions that the House has imposed upon itself in matters of confidentiality of committee reports, and consider carefully how any decision it might make potentially to breach the privileges of the House impacts on the important principles of parliamentary government and can do great harm to the public interest.

COASTING TRADE AND COMMERCIAL MARINE ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Legislative Committee on Bill C-52, an Act respecting the use of foreign ships and non-duty paid ships in the coasting trades and in other marine activities of a commercial nature has the honour to table its report in both official languages.
I should like to thank all members of the Committee for the extensive work they have performed during the past few weeks. Our proceedings were carried on in a climate of sincere cooperation, thus allowing us to improve significantly the bill under consideration.

I would also like to express my gratitude to all the witnesses who accepted to appear, sometimes on very short notice, before the committee, and to share with us their views concerning this piece of legislation. Their expertise has been very helpful to the committee.

maintopic: FINANCE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS-FIFTEENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
FINANCE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS-FIFTEENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present in both official languages the fifteenth report of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs in relation to the goods and service tax. This report deals specifically with the committee's visit to New Zealand between February 14, 1988, and February 23, 1988.
The committee held 22 meetings in New Zealand with the architect of the tax, the Minister of Finance for New Zealand, Roger Douglas, many of his colleagues, public officials, independent businessmen, legal and accounting people. In all we saw 37 witnesses. The report is a very comprehensive report.
Without going into the full recommendations, I might say for those who have leaked this report that the committee makes no recommendation with respect to the taxing of such necessities as food.

subsubtopic: LOW-LEVEL FLIGHTS OVER GOOSE BAY, LABRADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition from a number of residents of Canada who are concerned about the low-level flight training of pilots of NATO countries at the Canadian Forces Base in Goose Bay, Labrador. This is disrupting many of the native people whose lives are based on hunting, fishing, tourism, and mining, and which they feel provides a more stable, healthy, and peaceful employment there.
The petitioners point out that this program to train pilots to fly under radar into eastern Europe is a provocative and aggressive war-fighting action tending to endanger world peace. Therefore, the petitioners ask Parliament to ensure that the Prime Minister will end all low-level flight training at the Goose Bay Canadian Forces Base and cease negotiations with NATO for the establishment of a larger base there.

Mr. Speaker, 1 also have a petition from a number of residents of the constituency of Spadina. They point out that the fabric of Canadian sovereignty is threatened by the proposed agreement between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the United States, the Prime Minister having no mandate to negotiate such a deal with the United States. Furthermore, this deal would reduce Canada's ability to plan economic, social, and cultural programs that we need, and it would integrate Canada further into the North American defence industrial base.
For those reasons, the undersigned ask the House of Commons to ensure that a national debate takes place on this trade deal, and that this debate result in a national general election before any agreement has been signed.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition to present today which has been signed by members

of my constituency of Hamilton West and the neighbouring riding of Hamilton-Wentworth. The petitioners are members of the congregation of Westdale United Church in the City of Hamilton. Among other things they point out that, under successive Governments, Canada's weapons and weapon components industry has doubled in the past eight years.
They call upon Parliament to establish a review committee whose function would be to monitor Canada's policy in connection with this industry, and until such time halt further expansion of this industry in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present two petitions signed by Canadians from across the country. The petitioners are residents of Ottawa, Toronto, Edmonton, and Calgary. The petitioners urge the Government of Canada, and particularly the Minister of Immigration, to amend the legislation, Bill C-55, dealing with the refugee determination system, in order that the prescreening stage and the implementation of a safe third country would be removed from the proposed legislation and thereby make the legislation more fair, just, and equally effective. I table the petitions for the consideration of the Government and of the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present two petitions both of which deal with the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) trade agreement with President Reagan of the United States.
The petitioners object to the fact that the Government had no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a trade agreement with the United States. They object to the fact that the promise made in the bilateral trade negotiations that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised has been forgotten.
They humbly pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed trade agreement during a national general election.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (for the Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and President of the Treasury Board) moved
speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext:
that Bill C-79, an Act to amend the Canada Elections Act and other Acts in relation thereto, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to open what we hope will be a very short debate at second reading stage of Bill C-79. We want to get the Bill to a legislative committee where it can be examined in detail and where witnesses can be heard.
We appreciate that there is a continuing need to review the existing Canada Elections Act as a result of a recent committee hearing. However, we feel that Bill C-79, which has had a great deal of discussion among the Parties prior to this point in time, should proceed to committee in order to get the committee work started.
We assumed office in September, 1984. In response to various reports of the Canada Elections Commissioner, the Government began to review the Act and to consider various proposals for improvement. As a result of this exercise, the then President of the Privy Council published a White Paper on election reform in June, 1986, which announced the Government's proposals for reform of the Act. The paper was an important initiative of the Government. It served as the basis upon which constructive discussions developed among representatives of the three Parties.
I say without any hesitation that we have made a great deal of progress in trying to understand the legislation. I will discuss in a moment some possible amendments.
The legislation improves one of the most important pieces of legislation of any truly democratic society, that is, legislation dealing with the electoral process. It is for that reason that we moved slowly and in close co-operation with my colleagues in both opposition Parties.
I would say that we are confident that the result of this legislative revision will be to create a more fair and more equitable Canada Elections Act which is in step with not only the modern electoral process but with the changing needs of the electorate. A clear priority in the legislation is our desire to facilitate and extend the right of Canadians to vote.
I would suggest that one of the shortcomings of the present legislation in this regard-and I say it as a candidate and as a former campaign manager-is the problem encountered by urban voters who find, when they come to the polling station, that they are not permitted to vote because their names are not on the voters' list.

March 16, 1988
Canada Elections Act
In ridings such as Simcoe North we can fix that problem because people in rural areas are entitled to be sworn in at the poll. It is especially important when we have a summer election or an election in which the enumeration process took place during the summer. We find that people living in urban areas are, for some reason or other, not enumerated and therefore, if they do not catch it, not able to vote on voting day.
We think we have corrected that problem in the Bill. Often the problem is not a deliberate one; it is the result of an oversight or an error. After all, the point of the whole process is that Canadians should be allowed to vote, so we have included a solution in the Bill to correct present problems.
Let us move on to people who are absent from the electoral district on election day and inmates awaiting trial who are unable to get to their own polling station. We will make it easier, through the Bill, to vote in an advanced poll and easier to vote at the office of the returning officer whose office will be more accessible. We are also making it possible to vote in the office of the Deputy Assistant Returning Officer.
As well, we are giving federally-appointed judges the right to vote. There will be an enforcement commission to enforce the Act and to decide when prosecutions are necessary, and the trial will be held in a federal court as opposed to a provincial court.
There are other items in the Bill which I should like to highlight, for example proxy voting. It will be open to anyone absent from an electoral district on election day. However, we will not get into the business of wholesale proxy voting. It will be made an offence to solicit a proxy or be a proxy voter more than once.

Seasonal residents will no longer lose their franchise through restrictions to having to vote at their principal residence. They can now vote in the district of their second residence. This is a matter of great interest to a riding such as mine. Simcoe North has a great many seasonal residents who may wish to cast their vote where they are spending the summer. I would also say the same of the riding of the Hon. Member for Parry Sound- Muskoka (Mr. Darling) in that several residents would be in the same position.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext:
In any event, we are taking steps to accommodate the physically handicapped at all central polls, offices of returning officers, and advance polls. They will all be required to have level access. Other polls will have level access wherever possible, or an explanation from the returning officer will be required.
I would say on a personal note that there was some editorial comment on this item in The Toronto Star. I think it was well intentioned in that The Toronto Star was promoting access for the disabled everywhere. I would point out to those who are concerned about such access that the Bill does state that the returning office must have such access, but there are certain polling stations in rural or remote areas where there may be difficulties with access. I believe that that is taken care of in the enumeration. We have taken great strides to overcome the problem, and speaking on behalf of the Government, I would hope that this is something that would be addressed by witnesses at committee if they so desire. If there are any improvements we can make in this area, we are certainly open to them.

In addition, Mr. Speaker, the ban on the sale of alcohol on election day and on the solicitation of votes by non-residents of Canada has been repealed.

For some time there has been the feeling that to ban the sale of alcohol on election day hearkened back to a time when votes could be won with the use of alcohol. My friend, the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, and I come from tourist areas. We do not see that it is any problem to have alcohol sold on voting day and still respect the traditions of a free and democratic election.
There are other changes to the Act in which the House may be interested with respect to the returning officer and his ability to delegate his responsibilities. In an effort to involve young people in the election process and at the same time to provide employment for young people, one of the things we did was to allow the returning officer to appoint young people who are 16 and 17 years old as enumerators, as district returning officers or as poll clerks and allow them to go outside the official electoral districts to participate. We think this broadens the process and gets young people involved in the electoral process earlier. We feel that they can do the job. We have no hesitation in making that particular amendment.
We have made certain changes in the provision for the nomination of candidates. A candidate will need to have 100 electors sign nomination papers in order to file. Those of us in the House who have been through the electoral process realize that it is a very serious matter. We have no difficulty with what are often called fringe candidates, but we appreciate that running in an election is a serious business and we want to make sure that we have entirely serious candidates in the field.
March 16, 1988

We feel that these amendments constitute an important step forward for anyone who believes as we do that we must upgrade our legislation in order to meet the objectives and the aspirations of our times. There have been very extensive negotiations and discussions between the Parties on certain items with a view to improving the Act as printed. I point particularly to the question addressed in the Bill of the right of Canadians abroad to vote. We appreciate that because of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, this issue must be addressed. I can say without hesitation that my colleagues in the opposition Parties felt the need to address it as well.
I would suggest that we had trouble with the mechanics of how we could implement the system in fairness not only to Canadians living abroad but also to people trying to organize elections. We have had discussions with the Table Officers as to how the issue might be addressed. Originally I had thought that a reference could be made by the House to the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure. I was advised by the Table Officers that it might be easier, when this Bill goes to a legislative committee, and as I said we hope it might go this afternoon, to ask the Elections, Privileges and Procedure Committee at the same time, by letter,to specifically address itself to that part of the Act as a reference or as an undertaking of the committee. At the same time we would indicate at committee that we would amend the Bill to delete that part and let the committee come up with a workable way of addressing the problem. I suggest that that is one way that that might be dealt with in the spirit of co-operation.
We also looked at certain other items in the Bill and I would signal that we are looking at amendments to those. Specifically, we looked at the question of opinion polls. The Bill has certain provisions for the publication of questions asked, who paid for the poll, when it was done and the like. As a result of representations from the media and others, we found that certain parts of the media like the print media would be able to handle that easily, whereas the electronic media could not handle that information within the context of a broadcast. We are looking at some amendments to that, amendments which have been discussed with my colleagues.
As well, we looked at the difficulties of reporting cash flow and other items with local associations. We looked at what has been referred to as premature publication of results and the difficulties we face in a country as big as this where the polls are closed at eight o'clock in Newfoundland and some four and a half hours later in British Columbia. I think we will see some amendments to that provision at committee.
In an effort to facilitate the election, we dealt with agents at the poll. There has been a suggestion that there should be two rather than one, and we have no difficulty with that particular amendment.
We looked at the enforcement commission provision. I speak for my colleagues, I am sure, when I say that members of all Parties want to be sure that the enforcement commission is seen to be non-partisan and is made up of the best people

possible. We are looking at wording which would take out any suggestion of partisanship in the process of appointments to that particular commission.
I do want to conclude shortly to allow my colleagues to address the Bill, but I want to say something, if I may, on the report which was tabled recently by the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure. Hon. Members will recall that we encouraged the committee to examine carefully the subject of election expenses.

To that end, Mr. Speaker, the Committee summoned some Elections Canada officials who, as expert witnesses, explained some of the Bill's difficult and complex aspects.

In its report, the committee recommended that the Act be amended as quickly as possible so that it defines precisely those election expenses which should be the subject of spending controls and rebates. I think it is fair to say that all of us who serve in this House share this objective. We are all seriously concerned about any ambiguities in the Act in this regard.
In addition, I think it is self-evident that this is a matter of great interest to the public and the media and there have been increased demands for clarity. It is because we share those objectives that we are committed to trying to find a way to clarify the issue of election expenses.
There have been discussions among officials of all Parties with a view to resolving this matter. The discussions have not been finalized yet, but once we are in a position to finalize them, we will look at the relevant legislation as quickly as possible.
We appreciate the positive comments that have been made by my colleagues in the opposition Parties with respect to this Bill. We sought the co-operation and support of the Opposition and it is our sincere intention to continue to proceed, in a nonpartisan and constructive spirit, with a review of any remaining issues.
I can assure you that the Government is prepared to listen to all views, those of our friends opposite and witnesses in committee, with a view to improving the Elections Act. I urge the opposition Parties to expedite this matter to committee stage so that we can start hearing witnesses, and get a feel for the amendments which have been agreed upon so that they can be drafted and moved. It is in the best interests of all Canadians who vote and in the best interests of all candidates who run that the technical matters in the Bill which are not at issue be proceeded with so that the Chief Electoral Officer can make the required changes. Therefore, I urge my colleagues opposite to give a speedy passage to this Bill so that the committee can start to hear witnesses and do its clause-by-clause work.

March 16, 1988

I want to close by thanking my colleagues opposite for their co-operation at this point and I hope we can move the Bill into committee as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say first of all that as far as the Liberal Party is concerned, we welcome Bill C-79 as a step in the right direction. For the most part, the Bill proposes a number of relatively ordinary and minor changes to the Canada Elections Act, although in many cases, the changes will prove very convenient for Canadian voters. We are not talking about any major change in philosophy or policy with respect to the legislation. What we have here is mainly a set of recommendations by the Chief Electoral Officer, set forth in a 160-page document about the size of a dictionary or telephone book.
I agree there has been a lot of discussion among the Parties about reaching a consensus on the content of the Bill and expediting this legislation with the unanimity that has become a tradition in the House of Commons when considering changes to the Canada Elections Act, which means refraining from all partisan debate.
There was a great deal of consultation, and I want to thank the Minister acting for the Government House Leader for inviting my colleague in the New Democratic Party and myself to his office, to review some of the more contentious and delicate aspects of the Bill. There are several, and I will get back to these later on.
I would say that on the whole, the Government has done a good job. However, I think it is unfortunate the Government neglected to propose amendments that would have had the effect of clarifying the definition of election expenses. I will get back to this. I mention this right at the beginning of my remarks because what will probably sink this Bill is the fact that the Government wants to have it passed quickly this afternoon. Indeed, not so long ago the Minister wrote to me suggesting that perhaps we might agree to put up only one speaker per Party. This could have been arranged had the Government made it clear it wanted to amend the Elections Act to clarify the definition of election expenses, and to establish the difference between what we call election expenses and campaign expenses. Unfortunately the Government does not seem to be inclined to do that, so perhaps the Minister will have to show more patience because, having brought the matter up with Party colleagues and in our caucus this morning I must regretfully tell the Minister that a few of my colleagues will want to speak to this Bill.

It would be my pleasure to agree with the Minister's suggestion that we deal with the Bill very quickly this afternoon, but the fact that the Government has not seen fit to bring in amendments to clarify the definition of election expenses has spurred some of my colleagues to action. Some of them will want to speak on this Bill and try to convince the Minister of the importance, if not the urgency, of amending
the Elections Act to clarify the definition of an election expense.
Let us have a look at some of the issues in this Bill. Everyone agrees that there are some small housekeeping items which are not too contentious. There were in general six issues discussed among the Parties and we were able to come to an agreement and resolve our differences on all of these issues.
The Minister referred earlier to opinion polls. Bill C-79 wanted to impose on all media, whether electronic or print, the requirement that they provide all information related to polls, such as who commissioned it, the size of the sample, when it was taken, and so on. However, the electronic media told us that it is very difficult in the short time they have available, either on radio or television, to provide all this information. I would have preferred to have a standard for the print media and another one for the electronic media so as to make sure that both were at least obliged to provide some information. However, since the Government agreed to some of our representations, I agreed, with some reluctance, to drop this from the Bill. I think we can live with it because in good part we have to admit that the print media has been providing all the information for a number of years already.
With regard to local riding associations, there again our Party would have preferred, the proposal that donations over $100 to riding associations be divulged, receipted and so on to have been mandatory rather than voluntary. We think to propose a voluntary system is window-dressing. It does not solve the problem. It is an attempt to say we have dealt with the problem but it is not a real solution. However, you cannot win on all fronts.
We said we would have liked annual returns because if riding associations are to collect moneys subject to the rebate, it means the public at large has been contributing through taxes. In this case, not only do you want to know who gave money to the riding association in amounts exceeding $100, you want to know what the riding association is doing with the money. The Bill did not contain that requirement. There was no provision for mandatory annual returns by riding associations. We thought that if they were to benefit from rebates and so on, they would have to be on the same level as Parties and candidates during elections, all of whom have to provide a return and account for what they have done with the money. However, we agreed to the Minister's proposal that this could be removed from the Bill rather than have a proposal which is not perfect.
However, I would ask the Minister if he would not be agreeable to referring this subject to a committee. I think we could work on this, improve it, and come to a solution if it were.
I know the Minister is willing to refer the question of voting abroad. If this also were referred, and it is a smaller item, it could be done in the same package and it would take much less time than the other issue. Maybe we could hear witnesses, too. At the same time as they are dealing with voting abroad
March 16, 1988

perhaps they can tell us what they think about local associations having to divulge their donors, having to provide annual returns, and so on.
The Government had originally decided that there would be only one agent representing a candidate at the polls. This became a problem in my province because we have traditionally had two. I have to give credit to the Government and the Minister who has expressed willingness to try to get back to two representatives per candidate. It has been suggested that we could restore partially what was in the Elections Act, that is, that one candidate could have two agents at the polls, but not at the counting. In my province it is mainly for the counting that we want to have two agents. I wonder whether it would not be possible through amendment at committee stage to try to restore what is in the Elections Act because that would suit a major province of the country which has 75 seats. Perhaps the Minister would like to reflect on that.
With regard to Canadians voting abroad, in principle we have welcomed the move by the Government to allow Canadians who happen to live abroad to exercise their right to vote. We differ in that we think that the proposal in Bill C-79 is too wide-ranging, too much subject to abuse, and has been put together too quickly. This is the reason that some of us have suggested to the Minister that this be stripped from the Bill by way of amendment and that we have a separate reference to the committee. The Minister has agreed to this and I would like to give him credit for that. I believe that if we take the time to think about it and ask Canadians to come before the committee to give us their views, we can devise a better system for allowing Canadians abroad to vote.
We are talking about a large number of people. Canadians abroad in the U.S. alone amount to about two million people. That figure is probably double world-wide. Some people have Canadian citizenship just because they were born in Canada. They may have moved when they were only a few months old and may have never lived in Canada since then. This Bill would give them the right to vote. I do not think it is fair for someone who is not really a Canadian, although he may have Canadian citizenship, to have the right to vote I would like to know what my fellow Canadians think about this. I would like to give them a chance to appear before the committee and tell us where to draw the line.
Obviously to give only Canadian Forces personnel and people working abroad for External Affairs the right to vote is not enough. That is clear in my mind. There are a number of people on contracts with various companies, for example people working for Bell Canada installing a telephone system in Saudi Arabia or some other part of the world. Why should they lose their right to vote because they happen to be working abroad when an election is called?
It is a matter of determining who has the right to vote, under what conditions, and how to facilitate that. I believe that
Canada Elections Act
to refer this to the committee is the proper route. The Government has decided to do that and the Minister should take credit for that.
With regard to the enforcement commission, I and my Party are quite satisfied that we are going to change the way the Act is enforced. Very recently we had hearings before the Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure. Elections Canada was called upon to appear, and the Elections Commissioner was questioned on the procedures he uses to police and enforce the Act. Bill C-79 is bringing forth a whole new concept. We will now have not an Elections Commissioner but an enforcement commission made up of representatives of all Parties. I think that is a great step forward.
We have been discussing this at length among the Parties. I understand that the last proposal of the Minister is that the chairman and the member of the enforcement commission representing the public be appointed by a resolution of the House of Commons. I think that is fair. I think we should have another resolution which would contain in whole the representatives of each political Party as they are agreed to.
In devising such a system we would need, first, maximum consultation among the Parties. The last thing we want is a commission staffed with people who are there only to protect the interests of their own Party. We want a level of quality of people sitting on that committee which goes beyond the mere protection of the interests of a political Party. We want people with vision.
There is a risk with such a system, that being that if only people protecting interests are sitting around the table the temptation may exist to say, "We will not lay charges against your guy in such a riding provided you do not suggest that this guy of our Party in another riding broke the law". I do not think this is the way in which this should be approached. We want the type of people who are going to be impartial as much as possible. I want maximum consultation among the Parties at the time of appointment in order that we have a crew of five very solid and competent people who will do a good job for us and who will police the Act in an impartial way. I believe that to present the appointments in two motions like this in the House of Commons could go a long way toward providing this enhanced consultation.
I would now like to come to the other part of the proposal, especially the latest proposal made by the Minister in letters to us and also in the speech he just made. This is the more difficult part. We on this side of the House are saddened that the Government would not seize the opportunity of making extensive amendments to the Elections Act without bringing forward those amendments which, in our opinion, are most urgently needed.
I would like to refer to the extensive hearings which have been held by the Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure in the case of the election expenses of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse). We heard several witnesses and rapidly came to the determination that

March 16, 1988

Canada Elections Act
the Election Expenses Act is not clear enough when it tries, and I use the word "tries" advisedly, to define an election expense. I would like to quote some of the recommendations made in the eighth report of the Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure. It reads in part as follows:
The difficulty with the limited scope of the definition of election expenses was alluded to in a document produced by Elections Canada on 9 July, 1984-
-just after the last election-
-entitled Guidelines Respecting Election Expenses of Registered Political Parties. It was further amplified in a telex to all political parties on September 1,1984-
That was only three days before the last election. Maybe it was too late to change the Elections Act then, but three years have elapsed since that time. The Government has been reminded time and time again that there is a problem with the definition of election expenses, but it has not moved to correct the situation.
First, I was surprised it would not be included in Bill C-79, but let us be honest, Bill C-79 was written almost a year ago. But after the hearings of the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure, I cannot understand why the Government would not realize that there is a gaping hole in the rules defining election expenses through which one could drive a truckload of unreported election expenses, making a mockery of what I thought was the principle that election expenses were to be limited to give an equal chance to all persons running for election whether they be rich or have a medium income and medium means to run their campaign. The committee report states:
It was pointed out time and time again during the hearings that the present definition in the Act of those campaign expenses that are "election expenses" is vague and imprecise. Your committee is also concerned that the vagueness of wording and interpretation may lead to abuses during the next election.
That is clear enough. I would like to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, in case you may have been busy doing something else and was not able to attend this committee, that this is a unanimous report. The majority of the committee was composed of members of the government side, and this is a unanimous report. We all came to the obvious conclusion that the Act is too vague.
[ Translation]
And that being said, Mr. Speaker, the recommendation we finally made was again unanimous: Your Committee recommends that the Act be amended as quickly as possible in those sections dealing with expenses so that it precisely defines those election expenses which should be the subject of spending controls and rebates. That is crystal clear. I repeat that the Committee of which I was a member and with me, one of my NDP colleagues, nevertheless consisted of a majority of Conservative Members who in fact drafted the recommendation.
Furthermore, some Conservative Ministers commented on the Canada Elections Act, and I am thinking of the Minister
of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), who was glad the Committee decided not to condemn his actions following the hearings, possibly because the Committee failed to obtain all the information it needed, but in any case, although the Minister was vastly relieved, he did have some comments about the Canada Elections Act.
Mr. Speaker, I have here an article that appeared in Le Devoir on February 29, and I quote: Masse in favour of amending the Canada Elections Act which was used against him.

"Masse rails against election expenses law. Masse wants election rules simplified".

Upon reading these articles, we realize that here again, the problem is that the definition of election expenses is not sufficiently clear. I don't know what the newspapers will have to say tomorrow morning. I don't know what you will see on the TV News this evening, Mr. Speaker, or what we will hear on the radio. However, I am sure that all the information media will be amazed to hear the Government missed a golden opportunity to amend the Canada Elections Act by clarifying the definition of election expenses. Especially since an ad hoc committee consisting of Members of all three Parties, the Conservative Party, the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party, has been sitting for some time and made recommendations that would provide for a more acurate definition of election expenses.
We want to prevent abuses, and the investigation carried out by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections is quite clear on this matter. If the legislation is not amended, the door will be wide open for all sorts of abuses during the next election.
Mr. Speaker, the Committee hearings have demonstrated that it is now possible to have paid volunteers in an election campaign. A contradiction in terms, paid "volunteers"!. That is exactly the ruling which Elections Canada made in connection with certain election expenses of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who had paid representatives in the polling stations and other people working on his election a salary which was under the commercial value. The ruling of Elections Canada is to the effect "... that these election expenses are not subject to the limit. We now have a new term "campaign expenses".
From now on, therefore, we will have campaign expenses which are not subject to the election expense limit, and also election expenses.
Which means that anyone can exceed the imposed ceiling which is between $35,000 and $40,000, depending on the riding and the number of voters, by as much as $15,000 or $20,000 over the election expense limit. Which means that the spirit of the legislation is no longer respected and those who

March 16, 1988

have lots of money can spend a great deal by using existing loopholes which the Government refuses to eliminate.
Mr. Speaker, I have just said that we now have "paid volunteers" people whose expenses on behalf of a candidate can be reimbursed such as car-renting, hotel and food costs; these are not election expenses, because the person whose expenses are being reimbursed is considered a "volunteer". Fancy that!
Again, this means that people in the know who take the trouble of learning about these loopholes can easily spend some $20,000, and even more over their election expense limit, without being subject to any kind of sanction by Elections Canada. This means that there is no longer equality among the candidates.
We are coming back to the old system where there were no expense limit and where those who had lots of money had a definite advantage over those who had lots of ideas but little money.

I realize that Bill C-79 was written before all these committee hearings. I admit that. But what surprises me is that the Minister does not appear to be willing to move amendments at the committee stage-
