speechtext:
The Minister says it is not within the scope of the Act. If the Government wants to close the loopholes, the Government can. It can get another royal recommendation. In this particular case, the Government is lucky because it happens to have the support of both the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party with respect to closing the loopholes. Therefore, it would not be a matter of the Government having to work very hard in trying to reach the objective of clarifying the definition of an election expense. The co-operation is offered. If the Minister does not do it, that is when the co-operation may not be forthcoming. I do not know what the media will be reporting tonight, but I am sure it will be quite surprised, after having followed very closely the committee hearings into the election expenses of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, to see the Government is not moving to close these loopholes.
The people of Canada will be surprised because now everyone realizes. Very few people knew before these committee hearings that there were two types of election expenses, election expenses and campaign expenses. Now all Canadians know that. Now all Canadians believe that there should be proper definitions in the Act.
I would like to suggest something very precise and concrete. I do not just want to argue about the election expenses. I would like to propose a concept of what should be considered an election expense. The concept my Party would like to put forward is very simple. It is that everything should be an election expense unless it is specifically excluded, not the other
Canada Elections Act
way around. The principle should be that every dollar that is spent in a riding during an election, by someone involved in the election, is philosophically, as far as I am concerned, for the election.
There could be exclusions, and some of them are already there. I realize, for example, that the personal expenses of candidates have to be excluded. Transportation expenses of candidates have to be excluded. If they were not, as they have been all this time, then it means that candidates representing or running in large ridings, where sometimes the means of transportation is by airplane, helicopter, ship, or whatever else, would not be on the same footing as people running in a small urban riding such as mine where the size of the riding is more vertical than horizontal.
A number of other items which can be excluded include auditors' fees, candidates' deposits and legal fees. My philosophy is that any expense in a riding related to an election is actually done to promote a candidate. No one spends money just for fun during an election campaign. If something is to be excluded then let us have it in print, otherwise let us include everything.
There were discussions between Parties to try to come to some agreement as to what to include. For example, do we include the cost of polling? I do not mind. There are ways to do that. We can exclude the cost of polling. Polling itself does not promote a Party, it provides one with information. It is from that information that the Party can make moves to try to win the election. But certainly the mere fact of polling is not something that promotes a Party in itself. It is research. Either we exclude it or, as the Conservative Party has suggested, let us include it. But let us increase the limit that Parties are allowed to spend. I am easy one way or the other. We can agree on these things. I understand that the amount of money that can be spent by a political Party during a campaign at this time is about $7.5 million. If we were to increase the limit to include polling, then we are talking about an additional $1 million. Perhaps that is the way to go.
There were also discussions about fund raising expenses. Some say that if one is using what is called a home list of preferred donors, then one is probably not winning votes because these are people who have been on the home list for years. One is simply collecting money. I would be willing to agree that if a Party does that or if a candidate does that, then the cost of sending letters should not be an election expense. It could be out and not in.
However, if one Party or one candidate is prospecting by sending out thousands and thousands of letters across the country, then these are certainly election expenses. I refer especially to three-page letters in which some Parties talk in bad terms of other Parties with a single paragraph at the end stating, "We also need your financial support". There are ways to agree on what is in and what is out. The groundwork was

March 16, 1988
Canada Elections Act
done during discussions between Parties. All the Government has to do is to step down and to take its responsibilities.
The Government has brought in Budgets with which other Parties did not agree. They still brought these Budgets down. The Government has negotiated the free trade deal with the United States. Not everyone in the country agrees with this, but the Government has still done it. I do not see why the Government should hide behind an eventual unanimity of the definition of election expenses. I think that the discussions between the three Parties are advanced enough that all the Government has to do at this stage is to settle a couple of outstanding items and to come in with actual amendments.
1 can make a couple of other suggestions. The Minister is listening. He is sitting across from me with a smile on his face. If I have the Minister listening to me, then I am going to make a couple of other concrete suggestions.
One of the obvious problems is with the definition of election expenses under the electoral terms. I think we have a problem with the words "for the purpose of promoting or opposing directly or during an election a particular registered Party or the election of a particular candidate". The minute we use the words "for the purpose of promoting or opposing" it is a matter of interpretation which is very difficult to make. This paragraph should be changed. The words "during the election" can be kept. I agree that if one spends money three months before an election or two days after voting day then one is not influencing the vote. I am saying that the philosophy of my Party is that if one is spending money during the writ, then one is spending money and one wants to win the election. It would be easy to clarify this paragraph.
Further down is paragraph 2.1(f) which is the paragraph that allowed the Minister of Energy to escape by paying people and still calling them volunteers. This paragraph states that an election expense is the cost of acquiring the services of any person, including remuneration and expenses paid to him or on his behalf as an official agent or registered agent or otherwise, except where such services are donated, something with which we all agree. If the person donates the service then one cannot say that it is an expense. It states further " provided at materially less than their commercial value". That is where the problem lies. Because of this particular section of the Act, one ends up being able to pay people and to claim that they are still volunteers, which does not make sense to me. It does not make sense to most Canadians. If people are paid, they are not volunteers. This can be corrected by removing some of the wording such as "except when services are provided at materially less than their commercial value".
The Minister certainly has a basis on which to move in and close these gaps. I am asking him to do that. If he does not do that, Canadians will be quite dissatisfied with the exercise in which we are now involved.
All the rest is housekeeping as far as I am concerned. It is small stuff compared to the definition of election expenses. I plead with the Minister to move in. We are ready to continue
discussions. We have had discussions between the three Parties. I think that they have been cordial and constructive. I have been trying to offer in a quick fashion some suggestions to the Minister as to how we can better define election expenses. If the Minister has something else, something of his own, or if my colleagues in the New Democratic Party have suggestions, then we are willing to listen. We are willing to discuss and to sit down to try to plug these gaps. It would be regrettable if Parliament would miss such an occasion, and to use a euphemism, if Parliament missed a golden opportunity to close these loopholes and to prevent what the committee determined has to be possible abuse during the next election.
Unfortunately, our Party will have to line up other speakers to try to convince the Minister that this is the most important part of the Act. This is the part that needs to be cured most. I recommend for bedtime reading to the Minister a document which is not very long. It is entitled, "Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Elections, Privilege and Procedure Respecting the Canada Elections Act", otherwise known as the eighth report of the committee. That was tabled in the House on March 3. If the Minister were to read this, he would come to the conclusion that the Government has to move in now to better define what is an election expense. If the Government does not do that, it will be proceeding at its own expense.

Mr. Speaker, during the comments of the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault), the Deputy House Leader made some remarks. He was reacting to the fact that the Liberal Member who just spoke had suggested that perhaps we should be looking at amendments in committee in regard to defining the Canada Elections Act. I am not sure if the comments were recorded by Hansard, but the effect of the Minister's comments were that we could not amend this Bill in committee with regard to election expenses because it goes beyond the scope of Bill C-79. I believe that the Minister is correct. That is one of the major concerns that we have with this piece of legislation. It does not deal with what all of us in the House, the media, and many people in the country know to be a glaring error or a loophole in the present legislation.
There are many things that are good in this legislation. We have been lobbied quite reasonably by the Government and by other people to try to send this legislation to committee quickly. For example, I know that the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young), who has been active in handicapped and disabled issues for a number of years, has talked to people from those communities. They state that they want this legislation because it does help to improve their access to polling stations and other election offices during the process of a federal election. Today it is necessary to speak for that group in the House and state that we are in favour of that clause. We are in favour of many of the clauses contained in the 160 page Bill in front of us today.
March 16, 1988

During the last little while, some of the problem areas of Bill C-79 have been discussed among the Parties. We think that we have come to grips with some of the major errors or problems within Bill C-79. We have not finished with all of the problems of Bill C-79, and I will deal with that later on.
The fact that the Government has not moved on providing a definition of what is an election expense is so glaring that we cannot agree to the passage of this legislation at this time. Until the Government is willing to address the whole issue, we cannot accept the Bill. We believe that this may be our only opportunity prior to the next election to close the loophole made so public by the affair of the Member for Frontenac (Mr. Masse). Without closing this loophole, the 1988 or 1989 election campaign will be a wide open affair with no effective limits placed on expenditures.
The revelations made by the former Commissioner of Canada Elections in front of the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure last month indicated what a mess we have. It is essential that the Government agrees to the inclusion of all expenses inside the elections expenses limits. Exceptions can be made for auditors, deposits, and other similar expenses, but these have to be specified. Allowing for grey areas in those categories only makes the situation worse. Again, big money can play an issue in deciding the fate of Parties and individuals in the election. We propose a philosophy of "if it ain't out it's in". In other words, anything that is not specifically excluded from the limit must be listed and must be included under the election spending limits.
We recognize that that can create a problem because we are changing the rules. If it is necessary, we agree that the limits should be increased to ensure that most legitimate expenses can be covered, but still keep the philosophy of the 1972-1974 legislation which stated that there should be a limit on how much the Parties can spend, and that there should be a limit on how much each of the candidates can spend.
We are not alone in that opinion. The lawyers for Elections Canada who were asked to look at this issue issued their report on March 3, 1988. The law firm of Borden and Elliot in dealing with this issue stated:
In our view, the easiest and simplest means of defining "election expenses" would be to deem all funds spent by a Candidate or a party in an election as "election expenses" and then proceed, in subparagraphs, to enumerate those items of expense which Parliament does not wish to limit. The Act is presently structured in such a manner that the broadest definition of election spending is found in section 62 in the words, "any expenses incurred on account of or in respect of the conduct or management of the election." Based on our suggestion wording such as that should constitute the definition of "election expenses" and the exceptions should follow setting forth those items of expense on which Parliament chooses not to place limitations...
That is the legal opinion received by Elections Canada earlier this month. We believe that in the legislation which presently exists in the various provinces, including the Province of Ontario, there are examples of what could be used in the federal Canada Elections Act. Our problem is the following. Over the next little while Bill C-79 will be studied. It deals with the Canada Elections Act, changes to the Canada
Canada Elections Act
Elections Act, and for some reason the Government is refusing to act on what might be the most important Section of the Canada Elections Act, which is the section dealing with election expenses.
We have been asked by the Government to have faith that it will do something prior to the next federal election. Although the Minister has been very forthright with us in the House, I must say that we have no reason to believe that there will be changes to the definitions of election expenses prior to the next election. We realize that agents for the Conservative Party were aware of the problem as early as the summer of 1985.
We are aware that the lawyer for the Member for Frontenac was aware of the situation. We are also aware that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources read his letter from Mr. Gorman to this same lawyer. We are aware that this same lawyer represents the Conservative Party at the ad hoc meetings of the three Parties. It is that committee which has been looking at election expenses since the summer of 1986. Yet nothing has happened. We are in a situation where the Government through legislation tabled in the summer of 1986 was aware of the problem. At that time it sent the issue of election expenses off to an all-Party committee, not the House committee but the ad hoc committee of officials of the various political Parties. Nothing happened. There were many meetings, but no agreement was reached.
It is almost two years later, and three years since Conservative lawyers were aware of the problem, and there is no legislation that indicates that the definition of election expenses will be changed. I do not wish a "Dodge City" type of election in 1988 or 1989. I believe that it is possible, if the Government has the will, to introduce legislation which allows us to deal with election expenses. I am very disappointed that the Government did not do so at the same time as it started debate on Bill C-79, the Bill we are presently debating. Bill C-79 was first tabled in the House on June 30, 1987, almost nine months ago. Until one and a half hours ago there was no debate on this piece of legislation whatsoever. That means that the Government had no parliamentary time invested in this legislation.
The Government had nothing to lose by holding off the introduction of this legislation for another week or two in order to allow its officials to make a proposal regarding election expenses and to reintroduce a piece of legislation incorporating Bill C-79 and a definition of election expenses. It could have done that. It would not have cost the Government any parliamentary time, but it would have meant that the committee had proposed legislation before it with regard to election expenses and that we in the committee would have been in a position to make whatever amendments were necessary. However, by starting the debate without any reference to the committee on election expenses, the Deputy House Leader for the Government has precluded any possibility of the committee

March 16, 1988
Canada Elections Act
making any legislative recommendations or amendments to Bill C-79 that deal with election expenses.
Once Bill C-79 gets to committee, it will be there for a fair length of time. It is a comprehensive Bill affecting many groups in society. Many individuals and others will want to make presentations to the committee. In addition, because it is a comprehensive piece of legislation, it will take time for the committee to study it in a clause by clause manner.
If the committee is doing that during the months of April and May, when will it start studying proposed legislation with regard to election expenses? It will not.
The Government has been unable to come up with a definition of election expenses, after the investigation of the Hon. Member for Frontenac after the various legal opinions of which people were aware in 1985, after the all-Party study throughout the summer of 1986. It did not do so in the fall of 1987, and if it does not do so in the spring of 1988, I do not believe it has a commitment to come up with a workable definition of election expenses. I am afraid that the Government may have some ulterior motives for not coming up with that definition.
As we are well aware, the Liberal Party is seriously in debt. The Conservative Party has a very good bankroll at the present time. It also believes that it has the ability to raise more money before the next election. The Government represents the Party which has the most to gain by being able to spend considerable amounts of money that are not covered by the limitations on election expenses.
One has only to look at the 1984 election to realize how close the Government came to going over the limits. One has only to look at the accounts of the Hon. Member for Frontenac to realize that much more was spent in that campaign than the election limits allowed because of a glaring loophole.
The Government can survive as a Party with the present very loose legislation. It may help the Tories save one or two seats, three or four seats, or five or six seats. It may help them to have a very expensive national campaign, but that is not democracy nor the intent of the present legislation.
In the mid-1970s all Parties agreed that there must be limitations on the expenses of Parties and candidates. They wrote legislation which they thought was very thorough. Most of us in all three Parties believed that it was thorough as we went through the 1979, 1980, and 1984 election campaigns. We believed that we had a good piece of legislation and that we had stopped most of the loopholes. When most of us campaigned we looked at our limits, whether it was $30,000 or $40,000 in our ridings. We looked to see what expenses we had to pay and tried to come in under the limits. We believed that it was just legislation which would be enforced. We now know, as a result of what happened to the Hon. Member for Frontenac and the committee study, that that was not the case.
We have a situation presently where, for example, I could hire volunteers whom I could be paying $40 or $50 per day. As
long as it is below the minimum wage, we can get away with it. We can assume that such people would be working 16 hours or 18 hours per day. In some elections they work that long. They are called volunteers, but they could be earning $40 per day over a 50-day period of time for some $2,000 each. I could fly the volunteers in helicopters to each of my 63 communities. I could put them up in hotels, resorts, or whatever other accommodation is available. I could feed them and give them expense money. All that could be done and I would not have to declare one cent under the election expenses limitations.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext: What about CUPW?

The Government House Leader is joking or suggesting that perhaps CUPW does not have that money. I will tell him that we can raise a lot of money in my riding as we have in the past. However, despite the fact that we can afford to run a very expensive campaign in the Churchill riding, and despite the fact that many of our incumbents could do so elsewhere in the country, we do not believe that we should buy votes. We do not believe that the system should be so unfair that one Party can spend $150,000 while another Party or individual who follows the spirit of the law is limited to $35,000.
There are some people who say that that will not happen. As a result of the investigation involving the Minister of Energy, we believe that approximately $20,000 was spent and assumed to be campaign expenses which did not come under the limitations.
It does not take much work for a campaign manager or a party official to realize that if these items come under election expenses they will use up that money and come up to their election limit. However, there are many items which no longer constitute an expense under the limits with which they can do whatever they want.
It is not only the case in rural ridings such as my own where the spirit of the Act can be so abused. Let us look at an urban riding where it is close, where we know that any of the three Parties could win the seat. It is quite simple to move in a bunch of university students or others who would be quite happy to work for $2,000 over a 50-day period, to put them up in hotels in Regina East or Regina West, and to feed them so that there is a full-time army of people campaigning on behalf of a candidate. It is quite a legal situation.
Oh, oh!
I hear some rantings by an Hon. Member.
Rational comment.

If a person has a rational comment to make, he will make it from his seat. If he does not have a rational comment to make, he will continue to heckle. The point is that all three Parties in the standing committee said that we had to deal with the issue. Also the lawyers for Elections Canada said that it had to be dealt with.
March 16, 1988

Let me explain other things that were said by the lawyers for Elections Canada. They indicated that the definition of election expenses was so troublesome, cumbersome, and ambiguous as to make it virtually impossible for any candidate to know if an expense is an election expense and, conversely, for the commissioner to know whether the failure of a candidate to include certain types of expenses as election expenses in the return should warrant prosecution.
This was not political rantings. It was something that we all realized was a problem for any candidate who wanted to run an honest campaign or for any Party that wanted to run an honest campaign. It is even a problem for those involved in investigations and prosecutions afterwards to know what should have been done or what should not have been done during an election campaign. It is a major problem, and there has been no commitment from the Government that it will deal with this issue prior to the next election.
I believe I have made my point on that, but it is so important that we have a real definition of election expenses. As the Liberal spokesman who spoke previously indicated, right now a candidate could send out a fund-raising letter lambasting his opponent, talking about what he or she has done or should not have done, to every person in the riding. In the last paragraph there could be a little pitch for the incumbent, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), for example. That would not constitute an election expense. It could contain page after page of the most vicious partisan material and it could actually ask for money for a candidate, but it would not constitute an election expense.
The same is true of polling. While polling people, a candidate could ask most blatant partisan questions, basically playing a recorded message for a political Party, but that is polling and it does not count as an expense. Obviously we do not have legislation which protects the candidates, and it must be cleaned up. For us to go forward with Bill C-79 without dealing with that is for us to create election havoc.
When the Minister introduced Bill C-79, he did not give a firm commitment to deal with election expenses. There was no commitment from the Government that that would be dealt with in an acceptable manner prior to any upcoming election. There was an agreement that the issue be studied, but there was no commitment to bringing forward provisions which are acceptable to the Parties in time for the next election.
I know that I do not have very much time left in debate, so I will turn to other matters. One of the areas on which we have come to agreement is the reporting of financial accounts by local constituency associations. In the legislation, there was a proposal for voluntary reporting by local associations. We consider that to be neither fish nor fowl.
If the Government believes that the funds raised by local associations and how those funds are spent, funds quite often gained through election rebates or tax rebates, should be
Canada Elections Act
recorded, then it should not be a voluntary effort, it should be a compulsory effort. The Government has stated in Bill C-79 that it does believe that this should be reported. There are large amounts of money in local associations for which no one is accountable and there are no controls over that money. We do have a problem.
Obviously the Government believed that there should be some accountability, but for some reason, it has made the accountability voluntary. I know that the Minister of State (Mr. Lewis) is not only a lawyer, something which we do not hold against him all the time, but in addition to that he is an accountant. To have voluntary accountability is to have no accountability at all.
Those associations with clean records which are spending money in a manner that will not suffer from public scrutiny will be quite willing to report their accounts on an annual basis. Those associations like the one in the constituency of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) with over $100,000 sitting in an account or accounts somewhere do not have to report, even though we do not know what they do with that money. We do not understand why the accountability is voluntary. We believe, and to be fair members of the Liberal Party also believe, that it should be compulsory.
Since we wanted compulsory accountability and the Government wanted voluntary accountability, the Government simply decided to take out the whole clause. That is the Government's way of coming to a compromise on this issue. We regret that because again, this is a chance to clean up the Elections Act and to ensure that money raised through election rebates, taxpayers' dollars, or tax rebates, is accountable. The Government was moving in that direction, but for some reason it decided not to move far enough. We do not like it but we accept the fact that this clause will be withdrawn in committee.
The issue of Canadians living abroad being allowed to vote is one which all of us regret cannot be dealt with at this time. It is unfortunate that we have not begun to deal with the Elections Act until almost the end of the fourth year of the Government's mandate. It is unfortunate that the proposal made in Bill C-79 is so wide open that it creates a problem for all three Parties.
As has been mentioned before, the proposal in Bill C-79 is to let anyone who has Canadian citizenship and who indicates that he or she may eventually return to Canada vote in an election. Tie or she could have been away not only five, 10 or 15 years but 30 or 40 years, most of his or her life. He or she would still be permitted to vote in a Canadian election, simply by saying that he or she will probably return to Canada at some point.
We believe that there are too many road-blocks preventing Canadians who are legitimately abroad from voting. We certainly believe that those who are working for Crown corporations, the federal Government, NGOs or the like should be able to vote. We would also suggest that those who

March 16, 1988
Canada Elections Act
are on vacation for a short length of time should be able to vote if they can get to a proper place like a Canadian consulate or embassy. However, to open it wide up without any clarification is unacceptable.
We proposed that we limit the categories of people who would be eligible for voting. We also suggested that those who had been away for five or ten years without ever returning to Canada should not be allowed to vote, but those who had been back or had only been away for four or five years should automatically be allowed to vote.
We went through the exercise of trying to find a reasonable compromise, but we could not find one. Now it appears that we will have to send this matter to committee for separate study, recognizing the fact that it will probably not be resolved before the next federal election.
I was asked by one of my colleagues why this should not be open, that there would not be that many voters from abroad who would vote. I was told that for every person who had never returned to Canada who voted, there would probably be six or seven living outside Canada and who should be able to vote who would vote. That might be true, but we are talking about massive numbers of people. On the American side, over two million Americans who live offshore have voted. With our population figures, Elections Canada assumes that there may be about 200,000 people who do not live in Canada voting in a general election.
The problem with the legislation is that a candidate who runs in Broadview-Greenwood, Regina or in Thunder Bay may find that there are 2,000 or 3,000 voters who will vote on election day who cannot be contacted. The candidate does not know where they live, he has no indication of who they are and he has no means of communicating with them. Yet they will make a difference when it comes to whether or not the candidate wins a seat.
We want to see Canadians who legitimately work or live elsewhere for a short period of time be able to vote. Unfortunately, the Government has been unable to make a proposal and unwilling to accept the amendments we have suggested to resolve this matter. Rather than having a complete screw-up in the next election, I believe we may be forced into taking this clause from the Bill and studying it separately, realizing that the net result will be that many Canadians who should legitimately be allowed to vote in the next election will not be able to do so.
This Bill contains 160 pages and I will not be able to deal with all the problems in it. Let me deal with some of the problems that will be important over the next little while.
When the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure dealt with the problems of the Hon. Member for Frontenac, we saw a need to tighten up the election enforcement commission. This Bill does that. It prevents premature
publicity when investigations are taking place. It allows the commission to use investigators outside of the RCMP so that maybe things can be done a little faster. This also shows that investigators are more directly accountable to the commission so that you have some control over what they are doing or not doing. You are in a position to give them direction so that they are actually investigating what they are supposed to be as opposed to doing a wide open investigation.
One of the problems with the present system is that the commissioner calls for an investigation but it is the RCMP, acting almost completely separate and apart, which conducts the investigation. This is without, in many cases, reporting back to the commissioner for instructions or legal interpretations. This Act improves that situation. That is very important to a lot of people because reputations have been hurt in the past and investigations have not been as thorough as they should be. This is not because the RCMP is doing an inefficient job, but because the people who carry out the investigations are not in a position to know what the commissioner is really after or what has transpired in the meanwhile.
One of our main concerns is that we make sure the commission is secure from the taint of political patronage and that decisions on investigations or prosecution for alleged infractions is non-partisan. This is not in the legislation but we have been assured that amendments will be coming forward, and we accept the concept that the Chair and the Member representing the public be approved through a resolution of this House. The members representing the various political Parties should also be approved through a motion or some other means with the agreement of all Party Leaders. However, we have to know a bit more about that process to make sure it does not become open to abuse.
We are also concerned, and I hope the Minister is paying attention, with what happens when one member representing a Party resigns. How will he or she be replaced? In the initial step you get agreement of the three Party leaders for all three people. We are not sure what happens when one person resigns and we have to replace that person.
The Bill also called for one agent in each poll. All three Parties are used to the practice of two agents in a poll. Quite often someone is inside seeing who has voted and someone can come in to see who has voted so that when the various Parties are knocking on doors, encouraging people to get out and vote, you do not knock on the door of someone who voted three hours ago. For some reason the legislation is going to restrict us to one agent who, presumably, will have to sit inside all day and not give any information to the Parties. Obviously that would restrict the use of an agent. The Government has recognized the error of its ways and is willing to go back to two agents per Party. That is a good move.
With respect to opinion polls, at the time the Government was in real trouble it decided it did not want opinion polls too often during an election. It came out with a very strict definition of what must be done if you publish an opinion poll.
March 16, 1988

However, it became so cumbersome that it was obvious, while it was all right for the print media, it would make it impossible for a radio or television reporter to cover an election. You have to spend 10 minutes explaining what the poll was, the sample size, the questions asked, who paid for it and what-have- you. That could not be done in a 30-second clip. We encouraged the Government to make sure what would be required for the print media be fairly specific, because they have the space, and that there be a shorter form for the electronic media. The Government, for its own reasons, determined that rather than having a different requirement for the different types of media, it will pull the entire section dealing with opinion polls. In the long run that might be regrettable. I believe there is some advantage to having minimum requirements.
An Hon. Member has said something and I do not know what it was. It is government legislation which was going to require everyone to say everything. We are saying we think a minimum would be a good idea and in the best interests of the public. Since the Government has gone from an all to nothing position I do not see how the Conservative Member, who holds himself out as an Elections Act expert, can object when the NDP says there should be a minimum standard. The Government, in the legislation now before us, requires very detailed information on the publication of opinion polls. We are saying we need something but you are too strict with regard to the electronic media. However, we thought something could have been done which was acceptable, and I hope that in committee we will still find some middle ground.
The last area to be dealt with by negotiation among the Parties, and I always like to bring this forward so it is not done just in the back room and the public has some knowledge about it, concerns the broadcasting of results. The problem was this. We in the West, especially the far west, would be driving home from work when the polls closed in Atlantic Canada. Even before someone has gone home for supper, before they even think about getting dressed up to go and vote, they would know that in Atlantic Canada 30 Members of this Party were elected, 10 of that Party and two Conservatives. The same thing would happen when the polls closed in Quebec and Ontario. I am sure my friend, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), will agree that western Canadians have often felt that decisions were made prior to the West being heard from.
Under the current legislation we have a rule that you cannot broadcast results until the polls close in that part of the country. We have a problem because the Broadcasting Act says that those companies which provide cable TV cannot edit the signals. The Elections Act says you cannot broadcast the results before the polls have closed, and the Broadcasting Act says you cannot edit the signals. If you are getting signals from Atlantic Canada or Hamilton, obviously they are going to cover the election. The legislation suggests that we just remove the ban on broadcasting the election results so that they can be given out as soon as they come in from various parts of the country.
Canada Elections Act
Personally I believe that would be unacceptable to many people in the West. Depending on what happens in the next election, it could increase regional animosity. The Government decided it will live with the present system for another election. We will still prohibit the broadcasting of election results, but have not taken the further step of changing the Broadcasting Act to allow those companies providing cable TV service to edit out election coverage. I wish it had gone that step further.
That is possible because in this Bill we are not just amending the Elections Act. If you look through it you will discover there are about five or six other pieces of legislation being changed at the same time. The Government can change not only the Elections Act but the Broadcasting Act at this time in such a way that cable companies and others are not forced to break one Act or the other. We are putting those companies in a very awkward situation. We have the power to fix that up and I hope the Government will take that into consideration.
You have indicated that I have one more minute left to speak. There are two areas I want to cover quickly. The first is that despite the amendments to improve the ability of urban voters to be registered and vote, we still forbid urban voters who have not been put on the election list from voting on election day. We create all sorts of other situations. They can go to the returning officer's office and vote on election day if they are not registered. There are all sorts of ways and means that they can get on the election list between the date of the writ and election day, but they still cannot be sworn in at the polls.
I will give a very quick sample of the problem that creates. Just as the election was called in 1984, thousands of people who worked at International Nickel in my riding were laid off for the entire summer. Most of them went back to visit their families. Most of them come from other parts of the province or other parts of the country. Many of them returned to Thompson just when school started, which happened to be September 4. They were not on the list.
You may say that is an exceptional circumstance, but we have many summer elections and many shut-downs. We are having too many of them and this problem will increase. I believe that we in this country should be politically sophisticated enough to allow people with the proper documentation to prove that they are Canadian citizens and live in a particular riding to swear to their identity on election day and be allowed to vote because they are Canadian citizens living in Canada.
I find it ironic that the Act proposes allowing all sorts of people to vote who have never been in Canada for the last 20 or 30 years, but does nothing to allow people who, for reasons beyond their control, have been left off the voters' list. We are talking about many thousands of Canadians.
There is a proposal in the legislation to change the number of voters per poll from an average of 250 to a minimum of 250. That in itself does not sound like a problem but it is my

March 16, 1988
Canada Elections Act
understanding from some calls I received very recently that people who have been appointed as returning officers have been instructed to have a minimum of 400 or 450 people per poll. If that is the intent of this change to the Elections Act, it is certainly going much beyond the concept of a minimum of 250 voters per poll. I would prefer that the legislation specify what is meant in order that we do not have enormous polls.

Mr. Speaker, it is a curious thing that this legislation should be taking so long to get through the House when every Member here considers himself or herself to be an expert on the subject because they all got here by complying with this law and have an intimate working knowledge with a lot of its provisions.
I would like to begin my comments this afternoon with the general observation that there are in fact a number of separate measures which, in the course of this thirty-third Parliament, are dealing in one way or another with the electoral procedure and the democratic process. We have heard criticisms this afternoon from Liberal and New Democratic spokesmen about the fact that more is not being done in Bill C-79 to address the definition of election and campaign expenses.
It is a fact that there have been and will be a number of separate statutes before this House addressing the election process. We have dealt already, for example, in this thirty-third Parliament with legislation to modify the rules for electoral boundaries. Section 51 of the Constitution and the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act were amended as one step. Bill C-79, presently before us, is a second step. The indication by the Minister that there will be further examination of election expenses following the report tabled in recent days by the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure will give rise to a further area of consideration.
There are two other Bills, one dealing with the registration of paid lobbyists and the other with conflict of interest legislation which pertains to Members of Parliament, which I think must be seen as part of the whole fabric dealing with this general area of the health, procedures and nature of our democratic process. Another which is being drafted which I intend to introduce as a Private Members' Bill is the national referendums and plebiscites Act, which would be a counterpart to the Elections Act and would provide for questions to be submitted directly to the people.
I make those general comments only to set in a broader and fairer context some of the narrow criticisms which have been coming from the two opposition Parties about the fact there are some things not being dealt with in Bill C-79.
Speaking frankly, I share the regret that we are dealing with this only at this stage. I was chairman of the caucus committee on election law and redistribution which in 1984 and 1985 made recommendations that would result in changes. This became the White Paper and then the legislation. The series of delays has put the Chief Electoral Officer in an invidious
position. If we pass this legislation within the next month or so, and anticipating a reasonable date of June, 1989, for the next federal election, that would make it quite a time crunch for those who are shouldered, once this is passed, with the legal obligation of carrying out the election according to all these new procedures, rules and regulations.
I would like to turn to two or three specific sections that are included in Bill C-79 and stress their importance or significance. The first of those has to do with the position of disabled Canadians and their electoral process. Strides have been taken in previous amendments to this Act to, for example, facilitate voting by blind voters. The notch ballot in some jurisdictions and the template in other jurisdictions have been two of the technical methods used to facilitate blind voters to vote. There traditionally was also the way of being accompanied by a seeing voter in the ballot box area and marking the ballot that way.
In this Act we are considering amendments which will make further progress by ensuring level access to voting stations. When the Minister was speaking he pointed to the difficulties which exist in some of the rural areas. The provision which will be in this Act requiring enumerators to ascertain the level access requirement of voters will be helpful information, but more than that it will be necessary to ensure, in my view, level access for voters in every case.
I do appreciate that in some cases that may be an impossibility. I submit, and will in committee as well, that the answer to that is the mobile poll in the sense that the voting box and materials can actually be taken out and down the steps to facilitate voting by someone who is unable to enter the polling place.
Mobile polls are not a novelty. They were used in previous elections. Indeed, overseas, on those rare occasions when Canadian soldiers were voting during war time, ballot boxes were actually moved to where the soldiers were.
Another area which is significant in terms of Canadians with disabilities and voting is the extension of the franchise, under this Act, to Canadians with mental disabilities. The former prohibitions which existed in federal, and certainly a lot of the provincial statutes, were terrible provisions in the way in which they lumped people together and entirely disfranchised them on the basis of some mental affliction or disability.
When the equality rights committee of this Parliament met in New Brunswick, we heard submissions on the importance of extending the franchise to those with mental disabilities. Part of the rationale was that this in fact is a self-denying ordinance. Someone who is mentally incapable of getting to a ballot station and voting is not going to raise a problem, but there are many other individuals with some forms of mental illness from which they are recovering, which may create problems for them in their daily living, but do not in any way
March 16, 1988

impair their ability to follow public events and come to a very sound decision as to who is the best candidate or Party, and they should not be denied that basic democratic right. Therefore, I am glad this Act will reflect that more modern and compassionate approach.
I would point out that the Province of Ontario has already enacted such a provision. A provincial general election was conducted with that provision in place and it was a benefit to many and a problem for no one.
What represents a very important reform here is the establishment of the Canadian elections enforcement commission. A number of Members elected to this Parliament found, in the wake of the September 4 results, that investigations were being undertaken pertaining to their election expenses. In some cases those investigations were being conducted by officers of the RCMP. I have heard of some cases where the officers involved had just come off a drug bust, with much of the mentality used in dealing with thugs and criminals who are trafficking in drugs, and with a very combative approach to the "criminals" they were investigating. That was matched by a very shallow understanding, to put it generously, of the intricate provisions of the Canada Elections Act. That meant that there would be a significant difference in the perhaps 30 or 40 investigations going on across the country with respect to the level, quality and nature of the investigation. Therefore, the new provision which will allow the commission to appoint its own investigators, and to have a standard and uniform approach from coast to coast to coast by people who are knowledgeable about the Elections Act and the workings of the elections financing provisions, is going to prove to be in everyone's interest, including the public.
The provision in the Act that deals with liquor causes me to pause and take a drink of water, knowing that in future elections people will be able to pause and drink a glass of something stronger, because of the removal of the prohibition of selling liquor while the voting is under way. That provision is found there because of practices from the late 19th century when a great many elections saw a candidate floated to power on a perfect sea of booze. I know that in the Parry Sound- Muskoka district, where I come from originally, it took the Conservative Party many years to live down the infamy of the frozen whisky election campaign. Everyone here would know that whisky does not freeze because alcohol does not freeze. But in that election it did because it had been so watered down. When the voters came out from the schoolhouse to dip the metal bucket down into the barrel on the back of the sleigh out behind the school, the bucket did not come up with whisky, it hit ice. The whisky had frozen because it had been so watered down. For about a decade after that, the Conservatives in that area could never get any credibility or any vote because they were known to have watered down the whisky.
The more it changes, the more it stays the same.

I think that is another thing that speaks in favour of summertime elections. I am glad to see this Bill is
Canada Elections Act
going to committee with the full intention that a lot of these provisions will be thoroughly examined at that stage and further changes will be made. If we take, for example, the provisions which deal with the publication of opinion polls during a campaign, on the one hand, and the proposed removal from the Act of the ban on publication of election results in those areas where voting is still under way, we see something of a contradiction. First, dealing with opinion polls, I think the tendency in recent elections to have the publication of opinion poll results at different stages of the campaign has become, to some extent, a transforming factor in the way elections are viewed and understood. As much as there is concentration on the personalities, policies and programs, there is an emphasis on the polls, the reaction of the polls, and who is ahead and by how many lengths.
To see election campaigns transformed into horse races is not overly edifying, nor is it really that helpful to Canadians who want to see and hear about the candidates, policies and issues. That is why the recommendation was made that there be included in the Act something that I would really characterize as consumer protection legislation, that, yes, the major broadcasters and the major newspaper publishers do indicate who commissioned the poll, when it was conducted, how large the sample, the nature of the question and the percentage of error on a sample of that size.
We all know that there are other kinds of polls that are taken which may not be reliable. They may not be scientific in any sense. Yet they are reported on in the course of an election campaign, often with the effect of influencing or creating a lot of hype and getting a response to something that is as much a fiction of someone's imagination than it is an actual reflection of popular opinion.
Therefore, I think it is important to put within the Canada Elections Act this kind of consumer protection. If it is a difficulty for the broadcast media to do that in the course of a 30 second clip-the New Democratic Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) seemed almost beside himself in his concern about the broadcast media in this regard-perhaps it should not be trying to do it in a 30 second clip. Perhaps that is the answer.
We will look at that in committee and I would like to suggest that while looking at it, we should equally consider the proposal to delete the important section of the Canada Elections Act that prohibits disclosure of election results in an area where voting is still under way. The premature publication of election results can have an influence on the way others may vote. There are political scientists who argue for both sides saying that those who would jump on the bandwagon are counteracted by those who would opt for the underdog. However, we do not have to resolve that argument on a political scientific basis. I think we need to stick with the provision that was first enacted in 1938, primarily as a response to the practices of the Canadian Press. For years, the Canadian Press election report was Canada's only national compilation of the election results. Official reports available

March 16, 1988
Canada Elections Act
only weeks later did not name Parties, show Party standings or include Party vote compilations. The Canadian Press election reports became so systematized, thorough and fast as a tabulation of early accounts from individual constituencies that CP was able to flash the election or the defeat of federal Governments while voters in British Columbia were still casting ballots. Consequently, an Act was passed here in Parliament in 1938 to prevent publication of CP's results in either newspaper extras or on the air in any province while voting was still in progress. Something in the 1942 plebiscite on conscription contained the same provision.
In the 1960s and 1970s the broadcasting networks usurped this role CP had developed for itself, using their computers and nation-wide link-ups. However, the problem was still the same. This is why Section 105 of the Canada Elections Act, in a sense of preserving fairness, prohibits those publications in areas where voting is still under way. I think that is an important provision. I do not think it should be deleted. It is proposed that it be deleted, which is why I hope to speak to it in committee.
Generally, under this Act we are seeing a further opening up of the franchise. I have already mentioned the extension of the franchise to the disabled. The vote is now going to federal judges. There is also the proposal that Canadians living abroad be able to vote, much as Americans, Australians and residents of the United Kingdom are able to do.
We have also seen an extension of the franchise through the opportunities that are being increased under Bill C-79. It is worth pausing to record that Canada has the highest rate of eligible voters on its voters' list of any of the democracies. This is the reason we have the longest election campaigns, sort of a 58-60 day minimum. We are really the only country that starts about the whole process of compiling its voters' list after the election has begun. Yet that process ensures that some 97 per cent or 98 per cent of qualified voters find their names on the voters' lists. There is then a further period of revision, as well as courts of revision, which adds further opportunities for voters to find their names on the list.
In recent years we have taken additional steps to see that those who are thereby qualified to vote are not administratively disfranchised. It is one thing to be 18 or over, a Canadian resident and a Canadian citizen and therefore qualified. But, first, one has to have one's name on the voters' list. Second, one has to be able to actually get to vote at a time and place where the polls are open. That is why we have seen the provisions in this Act to expand proxy voting, to permit voting by people who have two residences. In the location of either one there is an option there to choose and so on. In other words, we are seeking to go the furthest route possible to ensure that every Canadian has the opportunity to fulfil their first duty as citizens which, of course, is to get themselves a government.
My final comment has to do with the concern being expressed by members of the two opposition Parties with respect to the definition of election expenses and campaign expenses. I share the concern expressed with respect to having this matter dealt with. I listened to the concern that was being expressed with two caveats in mind.
The first caveat is that the difficulties that they point out will, if unchanged in the present Act, continue to be difficulties that are shared equally by all Parties and all candidates seeking office and any effort therefore to parade these as giving some kind of particular advantage to one or another Party is to put on a partisan edge that really is inappropriate.
With respect to the second caveat, I listened to the concerns expressed with some sense of the history of Canadian elections when the way our great grandfathers and grandmothers conducted elections were wild in comparison to the almost genteel practices of today. The Minister from Newfoundland who is in the House knows that in his province, as in the Province of Quebec, there were election riots. In some of those election riots people were killed. Corruption was an absolute cornerstone of early Canadian elections. We have gone a long distance to bringing about changes, particularly in the 1974 legislation, to see that politics is not a rich person's game, that is it open, above board and fair to all.
With the reservations I have mentioned I think that Bill C-79 represents another important step forward.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member really believes that it is important to put everyone on an even footing and to establish very specific limits with respect to spending during election campaigns. Can the Hon. Member explain why his Government is not coming forward with specific amendments in relation to the definition of election and campaign expenses?

Mr. Speaker, I will repeat what I said when the Hon. Member was not in the House when I addressed this matter earlier in my remarks. I talked about six or seven different pieces of legislation that are going through the Thirty-third Parliament which deal with the various aspects of the electoral procedure. I referred to redistribution, conflict of interest legislation, the registration of paid lobbyists, Bill C-79 and my proposed legislation on national referendums and plebiscites that will be tabled soon.
Earlier the Minister expressed the intention to examine this matter, but he also said he had received an indication from the Table concerning the difficulties of dealing in Bill C-79, which has been in the House for quite some time now, with the subject matter of a report from the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure which was only tabled about 10 days ago. I think it is a problem of timing which has created an imperfect approach to this matter. However, I certainly join with the Hon. Member in wanting to see this other matter dealt with, if not in Bill C-79 then in other legislation.
March 16, 1988

Mr. Speaker, is the Hon. Member aware of the fact that the all-Party committee that has been meeting on the issue of the definition of campaign expense, et cetera, has in fact as recently as this week, put some agreement as to the definitions in these areas? It is my contention that if the Government is prepared to wait for a week or two in order to obtain some thoughtful and unanimous concerns in this regard then it can move ahead with the Bill that will deal with the issue of election spending. If this Bill goes ahead as is without the amendments that were blatantly called for in relation to the report of the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure, then obviously this Bill is a farce. If a situation exists in which, by statute, one can spend only, let us say for purposes of discussion, $38,000 on election expenses but one can go ahead and spend $60,000 or $70,000 on campaign expenses, then obviously de facto there is a free spending campaign which is in violation of the spirit of the Act. That is why I think the two have to go hand in hand. I think that they should be both brought together.

Mr. Speaker, I guess it is here that the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) and I part company rather dramatically. I think it is unconscionable that it has taken so long to get this Bill this far in this Parliament. The Hon. Member says that we should now delay yet a few more weeks because there is some discussion going on behind the curtains among the representatives of the three Parties as to what they might agree to as a definition of election expenses and campaign expenses. She suggests that we wait even longer to get on with measures that will give to disabled Canadians fair and greater access to the democratic process, as well as deal with some of these anomalous situations and outdated provisions in the statute.
I refer to measures with respect to liquor on the day of voting, and some of the other measures that I characterized as consumer protection legislation with respect to public opinion polls, and all the things that I did mention in the course of my speech. I regret that the Hon. Member for Hamilton East, who I know takes those things seriously, was not in the House during the course of my speech. She would have heard why I think it is truly unfortunate that at this late date we are going to be passing even this much and saddling the Chief Electoral Officer with the onerous task of gearing for an election on these changed procedures.
We must get on with this. Over nine months ago I proposed that this Bill be split in two and that the non-controversial parts be passed, and that those other areas dealing with broadcast and election expenses be delayed, if delay was necessary, to achieve a consensus in the House. I am no longer persuaded, on the basis of performance to date, that that type of consensus can or will be developed. I would resist strongly any effort to delay this Bill any further. There are many other good provisions in this Bill. I worked hard on it as chairman of the caucus committee since late 1984 and early 1985. The time
Canada Elections Act
to look for further causes for delay is passed, and the time for action is here.

I know the Hon. Member is one who had a great deal of input into the Bill before us. I would like to ask the Hon. Member for his comments with respect to four areas of the Bill.
First, one of the great areas of concern in the Bill certainly relates to having people enumerated and placed on the voters' list. Why is it that this Bill does not incorporate the provisions for a permanent voters' list?
Second, if there is not to be a permanent voters' list, in municipal elections one who is not on the voters' list can be sworn in at the polls on voting day at the time of voting. Why does the Bill not provide for that?
Third, traditionally judges have been considered to be entirely independent of the political process. Why does this Bill give, for the first time to my knowledge, the vote to judges?
Fourth, one of the penalties that has traditionally been imposed on those who are incarcerated is the temporary removal of one of the rights of citizenship, and that is the right to vote. Why is it that this Bill franchises people who are incarcerated? Having done so, if this legislation is passed, is it the intention of the Government, having franchised prisoners, to take away the right to vote from police officers?

First, the permanent voters' list has two problems. One is the cost. The cost is somewhere around $90 million to prepare an enumeration of voters' list in an election campaign. The cost of maintaining a permanent voters' list is in excess of that amount. Under our present system of enumeration, 97 to 98 per cent of eligible voters are on our voters' list. That is higher than any other democracy and that is because of the approach that we have.
In connection with national plebiscites, one of the inhibiting factors may be the cost of those votes. It would involve compiling the same voters' list at a cost of approximately $90 million. As a country, if we come to be more democratic and over the course of a Parliament submit one, two, or three matters directly to the people for their consideration, so that there are nation-wide votes at more frequent intervals, then it makes good sense to bring the cost of all of those votes down by instituting a permanent voters' list. That could also shorten the time of election campaigns.
Under the Charter there was a strong argument that judges not be disfranchised, but rather than we as parliamentarians making that decision on their behalf, should solicit even if informally through the channels and through the judicial councils and so on, a clear indication from the Canadian judiciary as to whether they want the long-standing tradition in this country to have our judges separate, apart and distinct from the electoral and political process continued, or they want to be on an equal footing with others and have the ability to cast a vote. To my knowledge, that course was not followed.

March 16, 1988
Canada Elections Act
The decision was taken, probably on advice of the Department of Justice, to extend the franchise to judges. Formerly the Liberal Party in Government amended the Canada Elections Act to give the vote to citizenship judges, but that was at a time when the appointment of those individuals was even more clearly identified with the Party affiliation and it was simply seen as a method of perhaps franchising a sure school of votes.
The question of the prisoners is one that was initially dealt with in the Province of Quebec where prisoners were given the right to vote in provincial general elections, and never in byelections. The issue is one that 1 felt was not ever adequately addressed by judges in passing sentence. It should be at that level where the judge is making the main assessment that the person is going to be removed of their liberty, and that at that level prisoners should have the vote taken away from them as an additional penalty.
I would like to continue, but I see that my time is up.

speechtext: There are three minutes left. On debate the Hon. Member for Hamilton East.

Mr. Speaker, very briefly I would like to call attention to our concerns in relation to campaign and election expenses.
If this particular Bill goes through as is, and I respect the intentions of the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer), it will be the greatest travesty to election expense control that has ever been levied on the people of Canada. It is a farce to claim that this particular Bill as is puts limits on spending. It sets up a situation which we have seen and identified where the current Act, because of its vagueness in relation to campaign expenses, will permit Members or candidates to go out and spend $100,000 plus allegedly under the guise that they are living within the guidelines that are set by the Act. This giant loophole has to be plugged. If it is not plugged, I would suggest that any talk by the Government about controlling spending is merely blowing in the wind, because it really has no intention of controlling spending unless it brings forward specific amendments to define campaign expenses in relation to election expenses.
I see that my time is up momentarily.
